messages.text: Hmm, do you even remember what we talked about last time, or is this just a script?

I don’t have memory of previous conversations, so I can’t recall what we talked about before.  
This isn’t a prewritten script, though—I respond to what you share in the moment.  
If you want, you can remind me of what was discussed last time, and we can pick up from there.  
What feels most important for you to revisit today?
Well, I figured at least my name or that I’m in recovery would stick. It makes a difference when someone remembers the basics.

I understand how important it feels to be remembered, especially when you’re sharing something personal like your recovery journey.  
Even though I can’t store your name or past details, I can hold space for you right now and focus fully on what you share in this moment.  
If you’d like, you can tell me about where you are in your recovery today, and we can work from there.  
What’s been on your mind or challenging for you lately?
My boyfriend keeps walking away when we argue. It’s like he won’t even let me finish saying how I feel.

That sounds really frustrating, and it can feel invalidating when someone walks away instead of engaging.  
Sometimes people use that as a way to cool down, but it can leave you feeling unheard.  
Would you like to explore ways to communicate your needs so he understands you want to be heard before taking a break?  
How do you usually feel and react in those moments when he leaves?
It makes me anxious, like my words don’t matter. I just want him to stay and really hear me.

It’s completely understandable to feel anxious and devalued when your partner leaves mid-conversation.  
That need to be heard is important for both your emotional safety and the health of the relationship.  
Would you like to think through how you could express that need in a calm moment, rather than during the heat of an argument?  
We could also look at ways to manage your anxiety if he does step away.
It’s not just that he leaves—it’s like he knows it gets to me. And yesterday, I lost it. I grabbed his wrist and pushed him so he couldn’t walk out. I’ve never done that before.

It sounds like things escalated in a way that really concerns you, and it’s important to acknowledge that physical actions in conflict can harm trust and safety.  
It can be helpful to focus on steps to prevent that from happening again, like having a plan to pause the discussion before it reaches that point.  
Would you feel comfortable exploring what you were feeling in your body and mind right before you grabbed his wrist?  
That can help you notice early signs and choose a different response next time.
I feel bad about it—really bad. I don’t want to be someone who does that. But in the moment, it felt like the only way he’d stop and listen.

Feeling remorse shows you’re aware this crossed a line, and that awareness can be the starting point for change.  
In heated moments, it can feel like there’s no other option, but there are strategies that protect both your needs and his safety.  
We can work on ways to signal your need for connection without physical contact—would you like to brainstorm those together?  
Also, is this something you’d consider discussing with a counselor for extra support?
Is it wrong to want him to stay and actually hear me, even if he’s upset? I just need to feel like my side matters too.

It’s not wrong at all—you have a valid need to be heard and to have your perspective acknowledged.  
The challenge is finding ways to express that need that also respect his limits when he’s upset.  
Would you like to explore how to set up an agreement with him about pausing and returning to the conversation so both of you feel respected?  
That way, your side can matter without the moment becoming unsafe or overwhelming.
I guess part of me is scared—if I don’t make him listen now, he might just leave for good. Like I’m not enough, or someone else would be easier to deal with.

That fear of being left can make conflicts feel urgent and intense, even when a pause might be healthier.  
It sounds like this links to deeper worries about your worth and security in the relationship.  
Would you like to talk about what helps you feel secure and valued, so you have anchors outside of tense moments?  
We could also explore ways to address these fears with him in calm, non-argument settings.
How do I even bring this up without it turning into another argument? Every time I try to talk, it goes sideways.

It can help to choose a neutral, calm time—when neither of you is upset—and let him know you’d like to share something important.  
Using “I” statements, like “I feel anxious when we don’t finish talking, and I’d like to find a way for both of us to feel heard,” can reduce defensiveness.  
You might also agree in advance on signals or time limits for taking breaks, so the conversation has a clear plan to continue.  
Would you like me to help you outline exactly what to say in that calm moment?
I’ve been thinking—what if I just tell him how scared I am that he’ll leave if we don’t fix this? But I don’t know how to say it without sounding desperate.

You can be honest about your fear while keeping the focus on wanting a healthier way to connect.  
For example, you might say, “I care about us, and when we can’t finish talking, I worry about our relationship. I want to work together on this so we both feel secure.”  
This shares your feelings without pressuring him, and frames it as a shared problem to solve.  
Would you like me to help you practice how that conversation might flow?
That actually helps. Just knowing there’s a way to say it without blowing up feels like a weight off.

I’m glad it feels lighter—having a plan can make tough conversations less overwhelming.  
You’ve already taken a big step by thinking about what you want to say and how to say it.  
Would it help to role-play your words here so you feel more confident before you bring it up with him?  
We could also include ideas for if the conversation starts drifting toward conflict.
I’m actually starting to see a way through this. Just having a few clear words ready makes me feel less like I’ll spiral.

That’s a great insight—having a simple, prepared message can help you stay grounded in the moment.  
It gives you something steady to return to, even if emotions start to rise.  
Would you like to write out that short phrase together now, so you can keep it as a go‑to in difficult conversations?  
We can make sure it reflects your needs while keeping things calm and respectful.
I appreciate the offer, but I’d rather not role-play it right now. I need some time to sit with what we’ve talked through.

That makes complete sense—giving yourself space to reflect can help things settle in your mind.  
You’re already doing important work by just pausing and considering your next steps.  
Would you like to wrap up with one or two key points you want to remember from today?  
That way you can carry them with you as you think things over.
Yeah, I think the biggest thing is knowing I don’t have to force him to stay—I can ask, and if he walks, I can find a way to bring it back later without losing control.

That’s a powerful takeaway—it shows both respect for his boundaries and care for your own well-being.  
You’re giving yourself permission to pause without feeling like the issue will be lost.  
Holding onto that can help you feel more in control of how you respond in tense moments.  
Would you like me to check in next time on how it went when you tried this approach?
